description: We are the team of five who enjoy conducting research and learning new things. In our project, we collected geographical surface data from Mars and the Moon and used these data to characterize a suitable terrestrial analog site.
summary:
TerraScope is a hybrid terrestrial analog site concept developed to identify Earth locations that can support research related to future Moon and Mars missions. We analyzed geological, topographical, environmental, and surface characteristics of the Moon and Mars and compared them with the Karapınar Volcanic Field in Konya, Türkiye.

Based on this comparison, we designed four complementary candidate areas: a basaltic plain, a crater/slope morphology area, a granular terrain area, and a water-rock interaction area. Each candidate is associated with a specific research question, such as rover mobility, terrain response, granular soil behavior, and geological processes.

Our project does not claim that Karapınar is an exact replica of the Moon or Mars. Instead, it provides a structured framework for identifying which terrestrial features can be used as analogs and how they could be validated through future field measurements and controlled tests.

TerraScope addresses the challenge by proposing a geographically connected, multi-feature analog concept that can support future planetary surface research while reducing the need to test every condition directly in extraterrestrial environments.
details:
TerraScope developed a preliminary hybrid terrestrial analog-site framework for the Karapınar Volcanic Field in Konya, Türkiye. The project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by identifying Earth locations where selected geological and surface characteristics of the Moon and Mars can be studied and compared before future space missions.

We first examined publicly available planetary data and compared the geological, topographical, and environmental characteristics of the Moon and Mars with published information about Karapınar. Based on this research, we designed four complementary candidate areas:

  • Area A – Basaltic Plain: Proposed for studying exposed volcanic surfaces, navigation, and rover mobility.
  • Area B – Crater/Slope Morphology: Proposed for comparing landforms, surface roughness, and slope-related conditions.
  • Area C – Granular Ground: Proposed for future studies of grain size, sinkage, traction, and wheel–soil interaction.
  • Area D – Water–Rock Interaction: Proposed for geological comparisons involving hydrovolcanic formations and possible alteration processes.

Our main outputs include a preliminary location map with reference coordinates, a Moon–Mars surface-feature matching diagram, a site-selection infographic, and comparative data tables. The four-area approach is creative because it brings different research questions together within one regional framework instead of relying on a single Earth analog.

The project can help planetary researchers and rover-development teams identify suitable locations for future terrestrial studies. It also provides a clear validation roadmap: defining site boundaries, calculating local slopes using DEM data, conducting geological and soil analyses, monitoring environmental conditions, and carrying out permitted, low-impact field tests.

We used institutional sources and open datasets from NASA, Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program, MTA, the Konya Governor’s Office, Mevlana Development Agency, USGS, and other relevant organizations. AI-assisted tools supported data interpretation, text editing, and the development of visual materials, maps, and tables. The scientific research, evaluation of evidence, and project decisions were carried out by the team. No custom code, hardware prototype, physical field experiment, or rover test was developed at this stage.

An important factor throughout our work was scientific accuracy: Karapınar is proposed as a candidate analog site, not an exact replica of the Moon or Mars. We also considered environmental protection, permissions, data reliability, and the distinction between documented findings and properties that still require measurement.
